problem: Existing EQA benchmarks (OpenEQA, HM-EQA etc.) assume every question is answerable, so agents are never tested on when to withhold an answer under missing, ambiguous or false-premise queries; forced answers lead to hallucination and unsafe behavior.
motivation: A 500-query human survey shows 32.4% of naturally asked questions lack sufficient context, so uncertainty is intrinsic to human-robot interaction. Hallucinated answers in embodied settings can cause physical harm, and ambiguous queries also derail navigation. Abstention is argued to be a prerequisite for clarification.
key_idea: Build AbstainEQA, a human-annotated benchmark with a five-type abstention taxonomy (grounded in Norman's cognitive error model) paired with answerable OpenEQA questions, to measure whether embodied VLM agents know when to say 'I don't know'.
insight: Frontier VLMs abstain rarely (best recall 42.79% vs humans 91.17%); scaling helps only within a family, and prompting merely trades recall for precision (HM-EQA fine prompt: recall 99.46% but precision 49.86%). SFT reaches ~83% recall, but text-only SFT, TF-IDF+LR and BERT match it (7B-Text-SFT F1 86.48 vs 7B-SFT 86.08), and randomizing images changes nothing, showing the models exploit lexical cues rather than visual evidence. Ambiguity also causes unstable exploration in A-EQA (SR 77.17→61.41).
method: Survey and quantification: 50 non-expert participants annotate 500 QA pairs over 152 HM3D/ScanNet egocentric videos; 32.4% found to need abstention (two annotators plus senior arbitration).

Taxonomy: five abstention types (Actionability Limitation, Referential Underspecification, Information Unavailability, False Presupposition, Preference Dependence), derived from Norman's sensing/interpretation failure framework.

Dataset curation: annotators write two ambiguous questions per type per video; 1,636 abstention cases paired with 1,636 answerable OpenEQA cases; A-EQA uses 3D-Mem's 184 questions with the original target objects kept; each question paraphrased into 5 variants by GPT-4o (16,360 QA pairs); ~460 annotation hours.
Frame-level annotation: Answer Frames for clear queries and Cause Frames for ambiguous ones, plus a short textual explanation of the evidence gap; reviewed by two additional annotators.

Evaluation protocol: GPT-4o as judge for LLM-Match correctness (1–5 score normalized to 0–100) and for abstention detection (Recall/Precision/Accuracy/F1); navigation metrics SR/TF/TS/PL following 3D-Mem; human validation (Pearson 0.88 on 300 samples, Spearman 0.89, abstention judge accuracy 0.92).

Benchmarked interventions: coarse and fine-grained abstention prompts, thinking vs instruct variants (Qwen3-VL 2B–32B, Gemini-2.5-Pro), and SFT variants (multimodal, random visual input, text-only, TF-IDF+LR, BERT) on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

setting.backbone: Evaluated off-the-shelf VLMs: Claude-Sonnet-4.5, GPT-5, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL (2B–32B), Qwen2.5-VL-7B; 3D-Mem with GPT-4o for A-EQA; SFT of Qwen2.5-VL-7B in the SFT analysis (benchmark paper)
setting.training_data: Benchmark paper; models are evaluated zero-shot. SFT analysis fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-7B on AbstainEQA data (split sizes not given).
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB video frames (EM-EQA) and active egocentric RGB-D exploration through 3D-Mem snapshots (A-EQA), plus a text question
setting.action_space: EM-EQA: text answer or abstain; A-EQA: navigation primitives plus STOP (3D-Mem frontier/snapshot-based exploration)
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D) and ScanNet scenes via OpenEQA/3D-Mem

numbers_note: Benchmark paper with no proposed method; numbers are baseline evaluations on the paper's own benchmark. Overall precision/F1 for the main models beyond Tables 4–6 are not given.
results: The best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, achieves only 42.79% overall abstention recall against 91.17% for humans (GPT-4o 32.09%, GPT-5 22.19%, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 1.04%). Prompting, scaling and reasoning give only marginal or trade-off gains, SFT overfits to text cues, and ambiguous queries drop 3D-Mem SR from 77.17% to 61.41%.
limitations: The benchmark diagnoses failures but proposes no method that fixes abstention or navigation under ambiguity.
Evaluation relies on GPT-4o as judge (agreement 0.88–0.92 with humans), and A-EQA analysis uses a small set of 184 questions (100 successful episodes for path analysis).
Abstention is evaluated only at the answer level; policy-level behavior such as when to stop or query the user is not addressed.
